questions.question: An open buffered channel has capacity 2 and already holds 2 values. A goroutine sends another value, with no receiver currently running. What happens?
questions.answer: B
questions.explanation: A full buffer makes a send wait; capacity is fixed. Fullness alone does not cause a panic.

options.text: The oldest value is overwritten.
The sender blocks until space becomes available.
The send immediately panics.
The channel grows automatically.

questions.question: Two receive cases in a Go select are both ready. There is no other code affecting readiness. Which statement is correct?
questions.answer: D
questions.explanation: select executes one selected case, not all ready cases. Source order does not assign priority.

options.text: The first case in source order always wins.
Both case bodies execute.
The case whose channel was created first wins.
One ready case is chosen pseudo-randomly.

questions.question: Two workers are registered with a WaitGroup before launch. Each prints its own label and then calls Done. Main calls Wait and then prints 'done'. What is guaranteed?
questions.answer: A
questions.explanation: Wait provides a completion barrier. It does not order the workers or limit concurrency.

options.text: Both worker labels precede 'done', but their relative order is unspecified.
Workers print in launch order.
Only one worker can execute at a time.
Wait cancels whichever worker finishes last.

questions.question: An InnoDB table has PRIMARY KEY(id) and a secondary INDEX(email). Which query is covered by the secondary index's stored columns?
questions.answer: C
questions.explanation: The secondary index contains email and the primary key id. name requires data not stored in this index; optimizer selection and MVCC details are separate concerns.

SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE email = ?

questions.question: A table already has many indexes. What is the main tradeoff of adding another index for a read query?
questions.answer: A
questions.explanation: An additional access path consumes storage and must be maintained when relevant data changes. Its value depends on the workload.

options.text: Potentially faster reads, but more storage and maintenance for writes affecting that index.
Faster reads and writes with no storage cost.
It changes the table's transaction isolation level.
It removes the need for statistics.

questions.question: Why does Reciprocal Rank Fusion combine ranks rather than directly adding BM25 scores and embedding similarities?

questions.question: What does ok=false mean in v, ok := <-ch?
questions.answer: The channel is closed and its buffered values have all been received; v is the element type's zero value.
questions.explanation: Closing does not discard buffered values. Those values are received with ok=true before closed-and-drained receives return ok=false.

questions.question: What is the distinction between commitIndex and lastApplied?
questions.answer: commitIndex tracks the highest entry known locally to be committed; lastApplied tracks local application progress.
questions.explanation: Commitment and application are different stages. Committed entries may still await delivery or execution by the local state machine.

questions.question: What is a back-to-table lookup when using an InnoDB secondary index?
questions.answer: Use the primary key found in the secondary index to look up the full row in the clustered index.
questions.explanation: It is needed for requested columns absent from the secondary index. A logical lookup need not be a physical disk read if pages are cached.

questions.question: Does UDP preserving datagram boundaries imply reliable, ordered delivery?
questions.answer: No. Datagram boundaries and delivery guarantees are separate properties.
questions.explanation: UDP does not itself guarantee delivery, ordering, or uniqueness.

questions.question: Why combine sparse and dense retrieval?
questions.answer: Sparse retrieval is useful for exact terms and identifiers; dense retrieval can match semantically related paraphrases.
questions.explanation: Their strengths are complementary. Improvement must be measured rather than assumed for every query.

questions.question: How does a typical cross-encoder reranker differ from a bi-encoder retriever?
questions.answer: A bi-encoder encodes query and document separately; a cross-encoder processes the pair jointly.
questions.explanation: Precomputed document embeddings make first-stage search efficient. Joint scoring spends more query-time computation on a smaller candidate set.

questions.question: Why does console.log(count) immediately after setCount(count + 1) read the old count?
questions.answer: The handler retains the state snapshot from the render that created it. The setter queues an update rather than mutating that local binding.
questions.explanation: A later render receives the updated state; the already-running handler keeps its original binding.

questions.question: When would a request counter belong in useRef rather than useState?
questions.answer: When callbacks need a persistent, mutable latest counter but changing it should not itself update the UI.
questions.explanation: A ref's current property can be read at callback execution time. State remains appropriate for data displayed by the UI.

questions.question:
What does this complete program print?

```go
package main
import "fmt"
func main() {
    ch := make(chan int, 1)
    ch <- 7
    close(ch)
    a, okA := <-ch
    b, okB := <-ch
    fmt.Println(a, okA, b, okB)
}
```
questions.answer: 7 true 0 false
questions.explanation: The buffered 7 is drained first. Only the next receive observes closed-and-empty.

questions.answer: No. Move wg.Add(1) before launching the goroutine.
questions.explanation: Wait can see a zero counter before the worker is scheduled and return immediately. Scheduling may also let the worker print, so there is no single guaranteed output.

questions.answer: No. Main blocks sending job 2 while the worker blocks sending result 2. Send jobs and close jobs in a separate producer goroutine while main consumes results.
questions.explanation: With one worker and unbuffered channels, neither side can reach its next receive. The sole worker may close results after jobs is drained because no other result sender exists.

rubric: Enables concurrent production and result consumption.

questions.explanation: The queue transforms 0 to 1, replaces it with 10 computed from the handler's snapshot, then transforms 10 to 20.

questions.answer: The next count is 1. Use three setCount(c => c + 1) calls to produce 3.
questions.explanation: All three value expressions read the same 0 snapshot and enqueue replacement with 1. Functional updaters consume the queued prior result.

questions.question:
An InnoDB table has a regular B-tree index on a DATETIME column created_at, with no functional index. Rewrite this predicate as a half-open range for the same calendar day. Assume all values and literals use the same time convention.

```sql
SELECT id FROM events
WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-11-04';
```
questions.explanation: The rewrite exposes a range on the indexed column and includes fractional seconds before midnight. It enables an access path but does not force the optimizer to choose it.
rubric: Does not promise a particular execution plan.

questions.question: Your Raft applier holds rf.mu while sending to an unbuffered applyCh. The application is slow to receive. Explain the risk and describe a safer single-applier sequence.
questions.answer: The send can block while holding the mutex, preventing handlers from acquiring it. Under the lock, choose and copy the next committed entry; unlock, deliver it, then reacquire the lock to record delivery progress.
questions.explanation: A single applier preserves ordered delivery while allowing consensus handlers to make progress. Coordinate this design with shutdown and snapshot handling; successful channel delivery is not necessarily completed application execution.
rubric: Identifies blocked send plus held mutex.
Preserves one ordered applier and distinguishes delivery from execution.

questions.question: Design the shutdown sequence for a finite worker pool: one producer, several workers, and one result consumer. Who closes jobs and results, and why?
questions.answer: The producer closes jobs after its final send. Workers drain jobs and finish their result sends, then signal completion. A coordinator waits for all workers and closes results; the consumer drains results concurrently.
questions.explanation: Closing results after all senders finish avoids send-on-closed-channel panics. Concurrent consumption avoids circular blocking; closing jobs lets workers exit their range loops.
rubric: All workers finish sending before results closes.
Does not require output order to match job order.

questions.question: A CS-note search misses both exact error codes and paraphrased concepts. Propose a retrieval pipeline and explain how you would evaluate it.
questions.answer: Retrieve with BM25 and embeddings, fuse their ranked candidates, rerank a bounded candidate set, then send selected passages to the generator. Evaluate candidate recall and final ranking on labeled queries, including both query types.
questions.explanation: Fusion addresses complementary matching behavior; reranking focuses the context. Compare against each retriever alone, track latency, and do not assume the extra stages always improve quality.
rubric: Uses complementary sparse and dense retrieval.
Measures recall and ranking with labeled queries.

questions.question: Design a receiver for a persistent TCP protocol with a 4-byte unsigned big-endian length followed by that many body bytes. How should it handle fragmented reads and multiple messages arriving together?
questions.answer: Accumulate bytes; wait for four header bytes; decode and validate length against a configured maximum; wait for the complete body; emit that message and continue parsing remaining bytes. Retain incomplete input for later reads.
questions.explanation: Neither header nor body must arrive in one read. EOF with an incomplete frame is truncation, and untrusted lengths must be bounded before large allocations.
